paras: The attempted lynching of Cliff Weeden was a near-lynching of a 13-year-old Black boy at Canton on a Monday evening in late June 1903, after he was accused of attempting to assault a 7-year-old white girl. Weeden escaped, and the episode is known only from a three-line item in the Savannah Morning News.

According to the item, Weeden was accused of an attempted assault on Maggie Rich, a 7-year-old white girl, on a Sunday afternoon. The report gives neither the state nor the county in which Canton lay, though it ran in a Savannah paper on a page carrying Georgia and Florida news.

On the following Monday evening, Weeden "had a narrow escape from being lynched" at Canton. The item does not describe who sought to lynch him, how many took part, whether he was in custody, or how he escaped.
No report of an arrest, charge, trial or later fate for Weeden was found, and nothing appears about action against those who threatened him.

The Savannah Morning News printed the story on July 2, 1903, under the headline "BARELY ESCAPED LYNCHING." In a single sentence, the item identified Weeden as a "negro boy" and the girl as white, and gave the accusation as the reason for the near-lynching without attributing it to any source. It offered no comment on the would-be lynchers, and no other white paper and no Black paper in the coverage carried the story.
